posts.title: The 63 tier list
posts.text:
America just got its 64th national park. Before Chiricahua gets a vote, here's how I ranked the other 63.

Yosemite is #24. Zion is #34. The Smokies, America's most-visited national park, are #51.

I stand by every single one of these. Fight me.

posts.title: The 63 tier list
posts.text: How the list works: every park scored 1-10 on scenery (40%), uniqueness (30%), crowd-to-wow (15%) and access (15%), out of 100. Ties go to better scenery, then uniqueness. Then 12 editor's moves, max 3 spots each, all with written reasons. Data: https://claude.ai/artifact/Js5RFzV6pZZ1xuC5Gasrfe

posts.text:

posts.title: The 63: the S tier, one at a time
posts.text:
Monday I ranked 63 national parks. A lot of you had opinions.

Here's the S tier, counted down. Six parks worth rearranging your life for.

posts.title: The 63: the S tier, one at a time
posts.text:
S tier, counted down.

#6 Crater Lake (OR): 1,943 ft deep, the deepest lake in the U.S., filled almost entirely by rain and snow.

#5 White Sands (NM): the world's largest gypsum dunefield (275 square miles), sand that stays cool to the touch even in July.

posts.title: The 63: the S tier, one at a time
posts.text: #4 Hawaiʻi Volcanoes (HI): the only park that keeps making more America. Kīlauea's lava flows have added brand-new land to the island, and Mauna Loa, in the same park, is the largest active volcano on Earth.

posts.title: The 63: the S tier, one at a time
posts.text: #3 Bryce Canyon (UT): fun fact, it isn't a canyon. It's a chain of giant natural amphitheaters holding the largest concentration of hoodoos on Earth, and the mostly flat Rim Trail lets you see them without breaking a sweat.

posts.title: The 63: the S tier, one at a time
posts.text:
#2 Yellowstone (WY/MT/ID): in 1872 the U.S. invented the national park, and more than 100 countries copied the idea. It still holds roughly half of the world's active geysers.

The formula had it #4. I moved it up 2 and will defend that in court.

posts.title: The 63: the S tier, one at a time
posts.text:
#1 Grand Canyon (AZ): a mile deep, 277 river miles long, and the only park to score above 90 (92.5 out of 100).

It's still the only view in America that makes a busload of strangers go quiet at the same moment.

posts.title: Chiricahua's verdict
posts.text:
Last month America got its 64th national park. I promised Chiricahua a verdict. Here it is:

70.0/100. #49 of 64. C tier.

A standing army of 27-million-year-old volcanic hoodoos, seen by about 70,000 people a year. It slots in right behind Badlands and bumps Wind Cave to #50.

posts.title: Chiricahua's verdict
posts.text: Same formula as the other 63: scenery 7 (40%), uniqueness 7 (30%), crowd-to-wow 9 (15%), access 5 (15%) = 70.0. No editor's override. That's 48th by pure formula; Acadia keeps its published +3 bump, so Chiricahua lands #49, the middle of C tier.

posts.title: The Thanksgiving Group Chat
posts.text:
The first Thanksgiving a U.S. president ever proclaimed was Thursday, November 26, 1789.

Tomorrow is Thursday, November 26.

Here's everything in between, as a group chat. Every message is a real quote. Receipts in the replies.

posts.title: The Thanksgiving Group Chat
posts.text: Receipt 1/3: Sarah Josepha Hale to Abraham Lincoln, 28 Sept 1863. By her own count she'd been pushing a national Thanksgiving for fifteen years. Lincoln proclaimed one five days later.

posts.title: The Thanksgiving Group Chat
posts.text: Receipt 2/3: Franklin to his daughter, 26 Jan 1784, on the bald eagle. He did like the turkey better, but he never actually proposed it as the national bird.

posts.title: The Thanksgiving Group Chat
posts.text: Receipt 3/3: FDR moved Thanksgiving up a week in 1939 to stretch the shopping season. Critics called it "Franksgiving." In 1941 Congress fixed it to the fourth Thursday of November for good.

alt.q1-question.png: Freedom Units question card: Lady Liberty's index finger is 8 ft long. How many of her index fingers stacked up would equal the copper statue itself, measured from the top of her base to the tip of the torch (151 ft 1 in)? Answer hidden.
alt.q1-answer.png: Freedom Units answer card: 18.9 Statue of Liberty index fingers. 151 ft 1 in = 151.08 ft. 151.08 ft / 8 ft = 18.89 From her base to the tip of her torch, she measures only about 19 fingers. Her pointer alone is longer than most people are tall.
alt.q2-question.png: Freedom Units question card: The Wright brothers' first powered flight on Dec. 17, 1903 covered 120 feet. How many 2023 Ford F-150 SuperCrew pickups with the 5.5-ft box (231.7 inches long each), parked bumper to bumper, would match that distance? Answer hidden.
alt.q2-answer.png: Freedom Units answer card: 6.2 F-150 SuperCrews. 120 ft x 12 = 1,440 in; 1,440 in / 231.7 in per F-150 = 6.21 Orville's 12-second hop was barely longer than six pickups parked in a row, and shorter than a Boeing 747's wingspan.
alt.q3-question.png: Freedom Units question card: The National Hot Dog and Sausage Council estimates Americans eat 150 million hot dogs on the Fourth of July. Assume each is a standard 6-inch frank. Laid end to end, how many times would they run historic Route 66 (2,448 miles, Chicago to Santa Monica)? Answer hidden.
alt.q3-answer.png: Freedom Units answer card: 5.8 Route 66s. 150,000,000 x 6 in = 900,000,000 in; / 63,360 in/mi = 14,204.5 mi; / 2,448 mi = 5.80 The NHDSC's own version: enough franks to stretch from D.C. to L.A. more than five times.
alt.q4-question.png: Freedom Units question card: Pour the 3.25 million cubic yards of concrete in Hoover Dam itself onto an NFL football field (360 ft x 160 ft, end zones included) as one straight-sided block. How many Washington Monuments (555 ft 5 1/8 in) tall would it be? Answer hidden.
alt.q4-answer.png: Freedom Units answer card: 2.74 Washington Monuments. 3,250,000 yd3 x 27 = 87,750,000 ft3. Field = 360 x 160 = 57,600 ft2. 87,750,000 / 57,600 = 1,523.4 ft tall. 1,523.4 / 555.43 = 2.74 A 1,523-ft concrete block, taller than the Empire State Building's 1,250-ft roof.
alt.q5-question.png: Freedom Units question card: NPS says the Mississippi River's average flow at New Orleans is 600,000 cubic feet per second. How many US gallon jugs of milk would that fill every second (1 cubic foot = 7.48052 gallons)? Answer hidden.
alt.q5-answer.png: Freedom Units answer card: 4,488,312 gallons per second. 600,000 cu ft/s x 7.48052 gal/cu ft = 4,488,312 gal/s The river only moves about 3 mph past New Orleans, but that's still about 4.5 million gallon jugs' worth every second.
alt.q6-question.png: Freedom Units question card: The Liberty Bell weighs 2,080 pounds, per the National Park Service. USDA's standard conversion says a gallon of milk weighs 8.6 pounds. How many gallons of milk weigh as much as the Liberty Bell? Answer hidden.
alt.q6-answer.png: Freedom Units answer card: 241.9 gallons of milk. 2,080 lb / 8.6 lb per gallon = 241.9 Lift 242 gallon jugs and you're hoisting a Liberty Bell's worth of weight, crack not included.
alt.q7-question.png: Freedom Units question card: Each presidential face on Mount Rushmore is 60 feet tall (NPS). A bald eagle's wingspan is 80.3 inches (Cornell Lab, All About Birds). How many bald eagles, wingtip to wingtip, would span one face from chin to the top of the head? Answer hidden.
alt.q7-answer.png: Freedom Units answer card: 9 bald eagles. 60 ft x 12 = 720 in; 720 in / 80.3 in per eagle = 8.97 Just nine bald eagles wingtip to wingtip would span a 60-foot face, about the height of a six-story building.
alt.q8-question.png: Freedom Units question card: NASA's Saturn V moon rocket stood 363 feet tall. Laid on its side, how many football fields long would it be, measuring a field as 100 yards (300 ft) goal line to goal line? Answer hidden.
alt.q8-answer.png: Freedom Units answer card: 1.21 football fields (100 yd). 363 ft / 300 ft = 1.21 Laid down at one goal line, a Saturn V would run clean through the far end zone and 33 feet past the end line.
alt.q9-question.png: Freedom Units question card: The Golden Gate Bridge's two main cables hold a combined 80,000 miles of galvanized steel wire. The Grand Canyon is 277 river miles long (Lees Ferry to the Grand Wash Cliffs). How many times could that wire run the full length of the canyon? Answer hidden.
alt.q9-answer.png: Freedom Units answer card: 289 Grand Canyon lengths. 80,000 mi / 277 mi = 288.8 The bridge's wire could run the whole canyon nearly 290 times.
alt.q10-question.png: Freedom Units question card: FHWA puts the Interstate Highway System at 48,830 miles (excluding Puerto Rico). The Mississippi River is 2,350 miles from Lake Itasca to the Gulf, the figure NPS's Mississippi National River and Recreation Area uses. How many Mississippi Rivers long is the Interstate System? Answer hidden.
alt.q10-answer.png: Freedom Units answer card: 20.8 Mississippi Rivers. 48,830 mi / 2,350 mi = 20.78 To drive every Interstate mile, you'd cover the Mississippi's full length nearly 21 times.
alt.s1.png: The 63, S tier, #1 of 63: Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona. It is a mile deep and 277 river miles long, and it's still the only view in America that makes a busload of strangers go quiet at the same moment.
alt.s2.png: The 63, S tier, #2 of 63: Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming, Montana, Idaho. The world's first national park still out-performs everyone, with half the planet's active geysers, bison traffic jams and a hot spring the colors of a rainbow.
alt.s3.png: The 63, S tier, #3 of 63: Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah. Thousands of orange hoodoos stand at attention like a stone color guard, and the mostly flat Rim Trail lets you review the troops without breaking a sweat.
alt.s4.png: The 63, S tier, #4 of 63: Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, Hawaii. It's the only park that keeps making more America, as Kīlauea has added brand-new land at no cost to the taxpayer.
alt.s5.png: The 63, S tier, #5 of 63: White Sands National Park, New Mexico. It protects most of the world's largest gypsum dunefield (275 square miles in all), and its white gypsum stays cool enough to sled on in July, which is the closest any American gets to landing on another planet without NASA.
alt.s6.png: The 63, S tier, #6 of 63: Crater Lake National Park, Oregon. At 1,943 feet it's the deepest lake in the country, it's so blue it looks photoshopped, and it fills itself almost entirely with rain and snow.
